html:
The Kalapuya are a Native American people of the Willamette Valley in western Oregon, between the Cascades and the Coast Range. They were eight independent groups speaking three related dialects.

They lived on the valley's prairies and oak savannas, which they kept open by setting fires every year. The fires helped the plants they gathered, above all camas, whose bulbs were a staple, along with acorns, hazelnuts and tarweed seeds. They also hunted deer and elk and fished.

Disaster came before the settlers. An epidemic, probably malaria, swept the lower Columbia and Willamette valleys in the early 1830s and killed most of the Kalapuya and their neighbours the Chinookan peoples. Then the Oregon Trail brought American farmers to the valley, to the very open land that Kalapuya fires had made. In 1855 the surviving Kalapuya gave up the valley by treaty and were moved to the Grand Ronde reservation. Today most of their descendants belong to the Confederated Tribes of Grand Ronde, and some to the Confederated Tribes of Siletz.
sum: The Kalapuya are a Native American people of the Willamette Valley in western Oregon, between the Cascades and the Coast Range. They were eight independent groups speaking three related dialects.
